analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to give full cash refunds for canceled or seriously delayed flights and for tickets canceled 48 hours ahead.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: after being referred to two House committees in July 2022, it sat in committee until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into law a right to a full cash refund, including extra fees paid, when an airline cancels or significantly delays a flight, or when a passenger cancels a ticket at least 48 hours before departure. Airlines could offer vouchers instead, but only if the voucher never expires and comes with a clear notice that cash is an option. Passengers who took vouchers instead of refunds during the 2020-2022 COVID disruptions could convert them back to cash. Airlines with over $1.5 billion in 2018 revenue and foreign carriers flying to the U.S. would face a $1,000 civil penalty per violation, and they would have to tell buyers before purchase that they can cancel for a full cash refund.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers. Anyone whose flight is canceled or badly delayed would get real money back, not an expiring voucher. People whose plans change at least two days out could cancel at no cost. Passengers who accepted vouchers during the COVID travel shutdown could reclaim cash. Because tickets must include the refund right, travelers would be shopping with clearer information.

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered airlines and ticket agents to offer a full cash refund, including ancillary fees, within 30 days of a request for a canceled or significantly delayed flight, or for a passenger cancellation at least 48 hours before departure [S2][S3].
Any voucher or credit offered instead of cash must remain valid indefinitely and come with a clear notice of the passenger's cash-refund right, ending the practice of short-lived vouchers [S2][S3].

Passengers who received vouchers rather than refunds for flights canceled between March 1, 2020 and enactment could request a cash refund to replace the voucher, with the airline complying within 30 days [S3].
Airlines and ticket agents must disclose, before sale, that passengers can cancel for any reason and get a full cash refund, giving buyers the terms upfront [S2][S3].
Violations carry a $1,000 civil penalty per violation, enforceable by the government [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large airlines and foreign carriers serving U.S. airports bear the cost: cash instead of vouchers on cancellations, a broad 48-hour free-cancellation window, retroactive cash refunds for COVID-era vouchers, and per-violation penalties. Ticket agents must process refunds but are entitled to prompt reimbursement from the airline for the airline's share of the ticket price. Some of these costs would likely be passed into ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: The right to cancel any ticket up to 48 hours before departure with a full cash refund goes well beyond current practice for nonrefundable fares; a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge is that airlines would likely restructure fares or raise prices to cover the added refund exposure [S3].
The bill only obligates carriers that had over $1.5 billion in 2018 operating revenue, so smaller carriers are exempt, creating an uneven rule between large and small airlines [S3].

The bill leaves 'significantly delayed' to be defined by the Secretary of Transportation rather than fixing a threshold in law, leaving the core consumer trigger subject to future administrative interpretation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — cash, not vouchers, when an airline cancels your flight — is real and modestly costly to airlines, which is why it was proposed during the 2022 wave of summer cancellations and schedule meltdowns. The most aggressive part is the universal 48-hour free-cancellation right, which would push up the cost of every nonrefundable fare and likely force airlines to reprice; the retroactive voucher-to-cash conversion is a one-time cost tied to federal COVID relief that airlines had already received. The balance favors passengers, with the caveat that the 48-hour window is broad enough that travelers would pay for it through fares.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees in July 2022 and to the Aviation Subcommittee in August, and neither committee brought it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 29, 2022 by Rep. Steve Cohen with 24 Democratic cosponsors, all from one party [S1][S4].
It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Financial Services Committee on the day of introduction, with no further full-committee action recorded [S5].
On August 1, 2022 it was referred to the Transportation Committee's Aviation Subcommittee, where the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended [S5].
No companion bill, floor vote, or chamber action appears anywhere in the action history; the Congress ended January 3, 2023, ending the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major airlines came out ahead: they kept the voucher-based refund system, avoided retroactive cash payouts for COVID-era vouchers, and faced no new cancellation-refund mandate from Congress.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 29, 2022 and assembled 24 original cosponsors.

for.name: 24 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans cosponsored.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill out of committee or scheduled a hearing or markup after referral on July 29, 2022.

against.name: U.S. passenger airline industry
against.what_they_did: Major U.S. airlines publicly resisted federal cash-refund mandates for cancellations during this period, having already argued they lacked cash during COVID; the industry's opposition was the backdrop for Congress not acting.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill received no Republican support on record; its referral to the Democratic-chaired Transportation Committee produced no action.

industries.note: Cash refunds instead of vouchers on cancellations, a 48-hour free-cancellation window, retroactive COVID-voucher conversions to cash, and $1,000-per-violation penalties directly cut airline revenue from kept fares and fees. Their interest in keeping vouchers and fare restrictions runs against passengers' interest in getting money back.

industries.industry: Foreign air carriers flying to and from the U.S.
industries.note: The bill covers foreign carriers operating U.S. routes, so international airlines would face the same cash-refund and disclosure rules as domestic majors, aligning U.S. policy with the stronger refund protections that exist in Europe.

industries.industry: Ticket agents and online booking platforms
industries.note: They must process refunds and add pre-sale disclosures, but the bill entitles them to prompt reimbursement from the airline for the airline's share of the ticket price, so their financial loss is limited to administrative burden.
